data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is true or probable, but as a methodological rule to select the theory with the highest empirical content and thus the greatest capacity for future falsification; this preference survives only if one accepts the cost of abandoning the goal of 'justified belief' in favor of 'optimal testability,' rendering scientific action a pragmatic gamble rather than a rational expectation of success.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude is strictly incoherent as argued by Miller and Tich\u00fd, then the link between corroboration and closeness to truth is severed, leaving the preference as merely psychological habit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies any expectation that the future will resemble the past (even pragmatically), it smuggles in the very principle of induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists act on corroborated theories because they believe them to be practically reliable, this belief constitutes an implicit probabilistic judgment, violating Popper's anti-probabilist stance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the procedural rule for theory choice (which maximizes risk). It posits that choosing the best-corroborated theory is equivalent to choosing the most severely tested survivor, which logically implies it has withstood the strongest attempts at refutation. This avoids induction because it makes no claim about the future performance of the theory based on past success, but rather selects the theory that currently offers the most precise targets for potential error. The defense relies on the concept of 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) as a regulative ideal rather than a quantifiable metric, acknowledging Miller and Tich\u00fd's refutation of its formal definition while retaining its heuristic value for directing research toward higher content.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
